title: Express and constructive conditions: editorial notes and questions
summary: Read the surrounding notes and questions alongside the principal cases. The complete assigned pages are preserved here.
notes:
Luttinger v. Rosen: This case separates a duty to make reasonable efforts from a condition that those efforts must actually produce a particular result. It also demonstrates how conditions allocate financing risk.

Peacock Construction Co. v. Modern Air Conditioning, Inc.: Peacock shows how transactional context and a default interpretation determine whether a clause creates a condition or simply fixes when an existing payment duty must be performed.

Gibson v. Cranage: This is the performance-stage counterpart to Mattei: a satisfaction provision can preserve a genuine choice while the nature of the promised result determines how that choice is judged.

Kingston v. Preston: Kingston supplies the basis for understanding why one party may withhold its performance when the return performance on which it depends has not occurred.

Jacob & Youngs, Inc. v. Kent: The case links substantial performance, implied conditions, forfeiture, and the choice between cost-of-correction and value-based damages. It explains why a breach and a continuing duty to pay can coexist.

Gill v. Johnstown Lumber Co.: Divisibility asks which parts of an exchange the agreement treats as corresponding units. It can reduce forfeiture without rewriting every unfinished task into a payable fraction.

Nelson v. Hazel: Nelson separates a breaching party’s failed claim for contract compensation from its possible restitution claim. A court can deny substantial performance and still prevent the owner from keeping a net benefit for free.

McKenna v. Vernon: Conduct during performance can change whether a party may insist on a condition, even though the written contract originally required it.
